titre: The Wildebeest, the Fire and the Tree: A Cattle Disease Held Back the Serengeti
accroche: For decades, rinderpest kept Serengeti wildebeest at low numbers. Its retreat changed the fires, then the trees.
contenu_vulgarise:
We know the images: hundreds of thousands of wildebeest crossing the plain, savannas dotted with trees, dry-season fires. We take them for the Serengeti "as it is." Yet, according to a 2009 analysis, this landscape has a dated trigger: the end of a cattle disease.

## A Cattle Disease

Rinderpest is a viral disease of cattle. Introduced into Africa in the late 19th century, it killed, by some estimates, 80 to 90% of the cattle of eastern and southern Africa in the epizootic of the 1890s. It also affects wildlife, wildebeest and buffalo. Domestic cattle are its reservoir, and periodic outbreaks kept bringing it back in the 20th century, which held wildebeest at a low level.

In the late 1950s, a vaccine becomes available. The government of Kenya systematically vaccinates cattle, and by about 1963 the disease is practically eliminated. According to a University of Vermont course textbook (working draft), the Serengeti wildebeest herd then goes, in about ten years, from some 200,000 animals to more than a million, then stops growing around 1975 at about 1.2 million. According to UBC Reports, Tony Sinclair (who devoted nearly forty years to this kind of research, about ten of them in the Serengeti) observed a sixfold increase in roughly fifteen years. These are estimates drawn from aerial sample counts, not full tallies: keep to the orders of magnitude.

## From Wildebeest to Tree

A million more wildebeest eat grass. Less grass means less fuel for bush fires. In 2009, Ricardo Holdo, Sinclair, Andrew Dobson and their colleagues test this chain on a 44-year series, from 1960 to 2003, covering the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem, about 25,000 km².

Their model finds that wildebeest grazing and the ratio of wet-season to dry-season rainfall are the best predictors of fire, the former weighing more heavily. It also finds that fire, and not elephants, mean rainfall or CO₂, is the main driver of changes in tree density. The annual rate of change in that density is negative from 1960 to the mid-1970s, then positive, with growth slowing after 1990. The model accounts for about three-quarters of the variance in fire and in that rate of change.

The authors describe what this changes: for wildebeest, we move from control by disease, which acts from above, to limitation by resource, the available grass, which acts from below.

## The Shift

The Serengeti of the 1960s, with its few wildebeest, more burned area and retreating trees, is therefore not a baseline state. According to this analysis, it is that of a system in which a cattle virus held wildebeest in check. In this reading, a major change in the park played out first in herds of vaccinated cattle.

The authors set limits themselves. They sought to reconstruct trajectories, not to establish what regulates wildebeest, and part of their carbon estimates relies on unpublished data. They suggest that the system, today a carbon sink, would have been a net source when rinderpest held sway: that is a model result, not a measurement.

What remains is a question this story poses for any notion of a pristine environment: pristine relative to what date?

repere.texte: A 44-year series (1960-2003) over about 25,000 km²: wildebeest grazing and the ratio of wet-season to dry-season rainfall are the best predictors of fire, and fire, not elephants, mean rainfall or CO₂, is the main driver of changes in tree density.
repere.source: Holdo, Sinclair, Dobson et al., “A Disease-Mediated Trophic Cascade in the Serengeti and its Implications for Ecosystem C,” PLoS Biology 7 (9), e1000210, 2009

carte.punch: The Serengeti of the 1960s was not a baseline state: a virus was holding the wildebeest in check.
carte.idee: When rinderpest was eliminated in cattle around 1963, Serengeti wildebeest became several times more numerous in about fifteen years. Less grass, fewer fires, then more trees.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Timeline of the disease and its global eradication, confirmed in May-June 2011.

quiz.question: According to Holdo and colleagues, how did the end of rinderpest ultimately affect the number of trees in the Serengeti?
choix: The more numerous wildebeest ate the grass, hence fewer fires and more trees
The more numerous wildebeest dispersed tree seeds across the whole plain
Elephants, less numerous after vaccination, stopped knocking down trees
Mean rainfall increased after 1960 and favored tree growth
quiz.explication: The chain the study retains runs through grass, fire, then trees. The other factors tested, elephants, mean rainfall and CO₂, have no effect distinguishable from zero on tree density. The other answers describe mechanisms the study does not retain.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is rinderpest, and when was it introduced into Africa?
choix: A viral disease of cattle, introduced in the late 19th century
An exceptional drought, which occurred in the 1930s
A parasitic disease of wildebeest, which appeared in the 20th century
An uncontrolled bush fire, set off in the 1950s
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rinderpest is a viral disease of cattle, introduced into Africa in the late 19th century, which killed 80 to 90% of the cattle of eastern and southern Africa in the 1890s.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What made it possible to eliminate rinderpest around 1963?
choix: A complete halt to cattle farming in the region
A mass cull of wildebeest carrying the virus
Systematic vaccination of cattle, carried out by Kenya
A ban on bush fires by the authorities
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A vaccine becomes available in the late 1950s; the government of Kenya systematically vaccinates cattle, and the disease is practically eliminated around 1963.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the model of Holdo and colleagues, what best explains changes in tree density between 1960 and 2003?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The model finds that fire, and not elephants, mean rainfall or CO₂, is the main driver of changes in tree density between 1960 and 2003.
